formatted_review:
The proposed Phase III clinical trial for Tanezumab, an investigational drug targeting RANKL, aims to assess its efficacy and safety in patients with moderate to severe osteoarthritis of the knee. The trial design features an open-label, parallel-group, randomized controlled framework with two treatment arms: Tanezumab 5 mg/kg administered every four weeks for a year, and a placebo comparator. The study plans to enroll 1000 participants, stratified by age, sex, and disease severity, ensuring a representative sample to enhance the generalizability of results. The primary objectives focus on evaluating pain reduction, functional improvement, and quality of life, with patient-reported outcomes as the primary endpoint.

From a regulatory perspective, the trial's medium risk profile reflects a careful consideration of both therapeutic potential and safety concerns. The mechanistic rationale underpinning Tanezumab's action on osteoarthritis through RANKL inhibition is well-supported by preclinical data. However, the long-term implications of RANKL inhibition on bone health warrant further investigation. To address this, the proposal includes a mechanistic substudy to elucidate these effects. Alternatively, advanced imaging techniques such as MRI or DXA scans are recommended to monitor structural changes as secondary outcomes, providing additional insights into the drug's impact on joint integrity.

The proposal's biomarker strategy is commendable, utilizing a blend of validated markers like serum CTX-I and BSAP alongside exploratory markers. This dual approach is designed to provide a comprehensive understanding of the drug's effect on bone turnover and inflammatory pathways, a strategy that has proven successful in other biologic drug trials. Should challenges arise with exploratory markers, the proposal suggests enhancing the statistical power of validated biomarkers, either by increasing the sample size or the frequency of biomarker assessments.

In terms of endpoints, the trial's reliance on subjective patient-reported outcomes is addressed by incorporating objective measures such as MRI-based cartilage volume assessments and quantitative sensory testing (QST). These objective measures are intended to complement and validate the subjective data, as demonstrated in previous analgesic trials where MRI and QST have provided crucial quantitative insights. If these measures prove infeasible, increasing the precision and frequency of patient-reported outcome assessments will be necessary to ensure data robustness.

Safety monitoring is a critical component of the trial, given the known risks associated with RANKL inhibition, such as osteonecrosis and hypersensitivity reactions. The proposal outlines enhanced safety protocols, including regular DXA scans, biomarker analysis for bone turnover, and vigilant monitoring for any signs of hypersensitivity or infection. These measures align with best practices from previous trials involving similar biologics. In cases where comprehensive safety monitoring is challenging, the proposal suggests implementing a rigorous risk management plan that includes predefined criteria for treatment discontinuation and enhanced patient education to promptly identify and address adverse events.

In conclusion, the proposed Phase III trial for Tanezumab is designed with a balanced approach to efficacy and safety, employing a comprehensive risk assessment framework. The trial's design and proposed strategies for risk mitigation reflect a commitment to scientific rigor and patient safety, addressing both the therapeutic promise of Tanezumab and the potential challenges associated with its use. The inclusion of mechanistic substudies, innovative biomarker strategies, and robust safety monitoring protocols are key strengths of the proposal, positioning it well for regulatory consideration. Should these measures be effectively implemented, the trial could provide valuable insights into the role of Tanezumab in managing osteoarthritis, potentially paving the way for new therapeutic options in this challenging clinical area.

14.4 Ankylosing Spondylitis
The efficacy and safety were assessed in 332 patients in one randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study [Trial AS-1 (NCT03928743)] in adult subjects 18 years of age and older with active ankylosing spondylitis. Subjects had to have documented radiologic evidence (x-ray) fulfilling the Modified New York criteria for AS. Subjects had active disease as defined by BASDAI ≥4 and spinal pain ≥4 on a 0 to 10 numeric rating scale (NRS) (from BASDAI Item 2). Subjects also had a history of inadequate response to 2 different non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), or intolerance or contraindication to NSAIDs. Approximately 20% of subjects were on concomitant cDMARDs. Overall, 16% of subjects had received previous treatment (failed or were intolerant to) with anti-TNF alpha agents.
Subjects were randomized 2:1 to receive BIMZELX 160 mg or placebo every 4 weeks up to the completion of Week 16 assessments. Starting at Week 16, all subjects received BIMZELX every 4 weeks up to Week 52. The primary endpoint was at least 40% improvement in Assessment of Spondyloarthritis International Society (ASAS 40) at Week 16.
Clinical Response
In Trial AS-1, treatment with BIMZELX resulted in significant improvements in the measure of disease activity compared to placebo at Week 16 (Table 9).

The recommended dose of ustekinumab was 0.75 mg/kg for subjects weighing less than 60 kg, 45 mg for subjects weighing 60 kg to 100 kg, and 90 mg for subjects weighing greater than 100 kg. At Week 12, subjects who received placebo were crossed over to receive ustekinumab at the recommended dose or one-half the recommended dose.
Of the pediatric subjects, approximately 63% had prior exposure to phototherapy or conventional systemic therapy and approximately 11% had prior exposure to biologics.
The endpoints were the proportion of subjects who achieved a PGA score of cleared (0) or minimal (1), PASI 75, and PASI 90 at Week 12. Subjects were followed for up to 60 weeks following first administration of trial agent.

14.3 Psoriatic Arthritis
The safety and efficacy of ustekinumab was assessed in 927 subjects (PsA STUDY 1, n=615; PsA STUDY 2, n=312), in two randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials in adult subjects 18 years of age and older with active PsA (≥5 swollen joints and ≥5 tender joints) despite non- steroidal anti-inflammatory (NSAID) or disease modifying antirheumatic (DMARD) therapy. Subjects in these trials had a diagnosis of PsA for at least 6 months. Subjects with each subtype of PsA were enrolled, including polyarticular arthritis with the absence of rheumatoid nodules (39%), spondylitis with peripheral arthritis (28%), asymmetric peripheral arthritis (21%), distal interphalangeal involvement (12%) and arthritis mutilans (0.5%). Over 70% and 40% of the subjects, respectively, had enthesitis and dactylitis at baseline.

The mean change from baseline to week 104 in Total Sharp-Genant Score for the tocilizumab 4 mg per kg groups was 0.47 (SD = 1.47) and for the 8 mg per kg groups was 0.34 (SD = 1.24). By the week 104, most patients in the control (placebo + MTX) group had crossed over to active treatment, and results are therefore not included for comparison. Patients in the active groups may have crossed over to the alternate active dose group, and results are reported per original randomized dose group.
In the placebo group, 66% of patients experienced no radiographic progression (Total Sharp-Genant Score change ≤ 0) at week 52 compared to 78% and 83% in the tocilizumab 4 mg per kg and 8 mg per kg, respectively. Following 104 weeks of treatment, 75% and 83% of patients initially randomized to tocilizumab 4 mg per kg and 8 mg per kg, respectively, experienced no progression of structural damage compared to 66% of placebo treated patients.
Health Related Outcomes
In Study II, physical function and disability were assessed using the Health Assessment Questionnaire Disability Index (HAQ-DI). Both dosing groups of tocilizumab demonstrated a greater improvement compared to the placebo group in the AUC of change from baseline in the HAQ-DI through week 52. The mean change from baseline to week 52 in HAQ-DI was 0.6, 0.5, and 0.4 for tocilizumab 8 mg per kg, tocilizumab 4 mg per kg, and placebo treatment groups, respectively. Sixty-three percent (63%) and sixty percent (60%) of patients in the tocilizumab 8 mg per kg and tocilizumab 4 mg per kg treatment groups, respectively, achieved a clinically relevant improvement in HAQ-DI (change from baseline of ≥ 0.3 units) at week 52 compared to 53% in the placebo treatment group.
Other Health-Related Outcomes
General health status was assessed by the Short Form Health Survey (SF-36) in Studies I – V. Patients receiving tocilizumab demonstrated greater improvement from baseline compared to placebo in the Physical Component Summary (PCS), Mental Component Summary (MCS), and in all 8 domains of the SF-36.
